nodes.summary: For elements $x$ and $y$ and a list $xs$, $x$ occurs before $y$ in $xs$ when there are lists $a$, $b$ and $c$ such that $xs$ is the concatenation of $a$, the element $x$, $b$, the element $y$ and $c$; that is, some occurrence of $x$ lies at a strictly earlier position than some occurrence of $y$.
nodes.title: Occurring before in a list

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a directed graph with ordered adjacency lists and fix an ordered list of roots. If $(c, p)$ is one of the (child, parent) pairs recorded by the left-first depth-first search of $G$ from these roots, then $c$ occurs before $p$ in the postorder (finish order) of that search.
nodes.title: A DFS child finishes before its parent

nodes.summary: For every directed graph $G$ with ordered adjacency lists, the whole-graph decreasing finish order of $G$ contains no vertex twice.
nodes.title: Whole-graph decreasing finish order has no repeated vertices

nodes.summary: For a directed graph $G$ with ordered adjacency lists, the whole-graph decreasing finish order is the decreasing finish order of the left-first depth-first search of $G$ whose roots are all vertices of $G$, taken in the graph's vertex enumeration order; its vertices are listed from the latest finished to the earliest finished.
nodes.title: Whole-graph decreasing finish order

nodes.summary: For every directed graph $G$ with ordered adjacency lists and every ordered list of roots, the decreasing finish order of the depth-first search of $G$ from those roots contains no vertex twice.
nodes.title: Decreasing finish order has no repeated vertices

nodes.summary: For a directed graph $G$ with ordered adjacency lists and an ordered list of roots, the decreasing finish order is the reverse of the postorder of the left-first depth-first search of $G$ from those roots: the vertices that search visits, listed from the latest finished to the earliest finished.
nodes.title: Decreasing finish order

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph whose vertices are listed without repetition as $v_1, \dots, v_n$, with ordered adjacency lists $N(v)$ whose entries may repeat. Run the depth-first search machine with roots $v_1, \dots, v_n$ in this order (each transition drops a pending vertex that is already visited, discovers a new vertex, or finishes a vertex). Then there is a terminal machine state, with no work left, whose…
nodes.title: Exact transition count of whole-graph depth-first search

nodes.summary: For a directed graph $G$ with ordered adjacency lists, the whole-graph traversal is the left-first depth-first search of $G$ whose roots are all vertices of $G$, taken in the graph's fixed vertex enumeration order.
nodes.title: Depth-first search of the whole graph

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph with ordered adjacency lists $N(v)$, whose entries may repeat, and let $R$ be a list of roots, possibly with repetitions. Run the depth-first search machine from $R$ (each transition drops a pending vertex that is already visited, discovers a new vertex, or finishes a vertex). Let $v_1, \dots, v_k$ be the preorder of the depth-first search of $G$ from $R$. Then there is a terminal…
nodes.title: Exact transition count of depth-first search

nodes.summary: For every directed graph $G$ with ordered adjacency lists and every ordered list of roots, the traversal computed by left-first depth-first search of $G$ from these roots conforms to left-first DFS for $G$ and these roots.
nodes.title: Executable DFS meets the left-first specification

nodes.summary: Given a directed graph $G$ with ordered adjacency lists and an ordered list of roots, depth-first search processes the roots from left to right, skipping roots already visited. Visiting an unvisited vertex $v$ marks it visited and records its discovery, then processes the out-neighbours of $v$ in adjacency-list order, visiting each one not yet visited at that moment and recording $v$ as its parent, and finally…
nodes.title: Left-first depth-first search

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a directed graph with ordered adjacency lists, fix an ordered list of roots, and let $T$ be a traversal. If $T$ conforms to left-first DFS for $G$ and these roots, then $T$ equals the traversal computed by left-first depth-first search of $G$ from these roots.
nodes.title: The left-first DFS specification determines the traversal

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph given by ordered adjacency lists, let $r$ be a list of root vertices, and let $v$ and $p$ be vertices. If $v$ is a forest root of the left-first depth-first search of $G$ from $r$, then $(v, p)$ is not among the (child, parent) pairs recorded by that search.
nodes.title: A DFS forest root has no parent

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph given by ordered adjacency lists, let $r$ be a list of root vertices, and let $v$ be a vertex. If $v$ is a forest root of the left-first depth-first search of $G$ from $r$, then $v$ occurs in $r$.
nodes.title: DFS forest roots are scheduled roots

nodes.summary: For every finite directed graph $G$ given by ordered adjacency lists and every list $r$ of root vertices, the list of forest roots of the left-first depth-first search of $G$ from $r$ contains no vertex twice.
nodes.title: DFS forest roots are distinct

nodes.summary: The forest roots of a traversal $T$ are the vertices of the preorder of $T$ that do not occur as the child in any (child, parent) pair recorded by $T$, listed in the order in which they occur in the preorder.
nodes.title: Roots of a DFS forest

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph given by ordered adjacency lists and let $r = (r_1, \dots, r_k)$ be a list of root vertices. A traversal $T$ is a left-first DFS of $G$ from $r$ when some finite run of the following machine ends with an empty work list and with recorded preorder, postorder and (child, parent) list equal to those of $T$.
nodes.title: Left-first depth-first traversals

nodes.summary: For every finite directed graph $G$ given by ordered adjacency lists and every vertex $v$ of $G$, $v$ occurs in the whole-graph decreasing finish order of $G$, that is, the decreasing finish order of the left-first depth-first search of $G$ whose roots are all vertices of $G$ in the graph's vertex order.
nodes.title: Whole-graph decreasing finish order contains every vertex

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph given by ordered adjacency lists, let $r$ be a list of root vertices, and let $v$ be a vertex. Then $v$ occurs in the decreasing finish order of the left-first depth-first search of $G$ from $r$ if and only if $v$ is reachable in $G$ from some vertex of $r$.
nodes.title: Decreasing finish order lists exactly the vertices reachable from the roots

nodes.summary: For every finite directed graph $G$ given by ordered adjacency lists and every vertex $v$ of $G$, $v$ occurs in the postorder of the whole-graph depth-first search of $G$, that is, the left-first depth-first search of $G$ whose roots are all vertices of $G$ in the graph's vertex order.
nodes.title: Whole-graph DFS finishes every vertex

nodes.summary: For every finite directed graph $G$ given by ordered adjacency lists and every vertex $v$ of $G$, $v$ occurs in the preorder of the whole-graph depth-first search of $G$, that is, the left-first depth-first search of $G$ whose roots are all vertices of $G$ in the graph's vertex order.
nodes.title: Whole-graph DFS discovers every vertex

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph given by ordered adjacency lists, let $r$ be a list of root vertices, and let $v$ be a vertex in the preorder of the left-first depth-first search of $G$ from $r$. Then $v$ is a forest root of that search, or there is exactly one vertex $p$ such that $(v, p)$ is among the (child, parent) pairs recorded by the search.
nodes.title: Every discovered vertex is a forest root or has a unique parent

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph and $R$ a list of root vertices. A vertex $v$ occurs in the finish order (postorder) of the depth-first search of $G$ from $R$ if and only if there is a root $r$ in $R$ from which $v$ is reachable in $G$ by a directed path of length zero or more.
nodes.title: Depth-first search finishes exactly the reachable vertices

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph and $R$ a list of root vertices. A vertex $v$ occurs in the discovery order (preorder) of the depth-first search of $G$ from $R$ if and only if there is a root $r$ in $R$ from which $v$ is reachable in $G$ by a directed path of length zero or more.
nodes.title: Depth-first search discovers exactly the reachable vertices

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph and $R$ a list of root vertices, and run depth-first search on $G$ from $R$. If the pair $(c, p)$ occurs in the list of (child, parent) pairs recorded by the search, then $p$ occurs strictly before $c$ in the decreasing finish order, the reverse of the finish order.
nodes.title: In decreasing finish order, a DFS parent precedes its child

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph and $R$ a list of root vertices, and run depth-first search on $G$ from $R$. If the pair $(c, p)$ occurs in the list of (child, parent) pairs recorded by the search, then $p$ occurs strictly before $c$ in the discovery order (preorder) of the search.
nodes.title: In preorder, a DFS parent precedes its child

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph and $R$ a list of root vertices, and run depth-first search on $G$ from $R$. Say that $p$ is a recorded parent of $c$ when the pair $(c, p)$ occurs in the list of (child, parent) pairs recorded by the search, and call a discovered vertex with no recorded parent a forest root. Then for every vertex $v$ in the discovery order (preorder) there are $k \ge 0$ and vertices…
nodes.title: Parent chains in a DFS forest end at a forest root

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph and $R$ a list of root vertices, and run depth-first search on $G$ from $R$. In the list of (child, parent) pairs recorded by the search, no vertex occurs as the child of more than one entry; that is, the list of children has no repeated entries.
nodes.title: No vertex is recorded twice as a DFS child

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph and $R$ a list of root vertices, and run depth-first search on $G$ from $R$. If the pair $(c, p)$ occurs in the list of (child, parent) pairs recorded by the search, then $G$ has a directed edge from $p$ to $c$.
nodes.title: DFS parent pairs are graph edges

nodes.summary: Given a list $P$ of (child, parent) pairs, $p$ is a parent of $c$ in $P$ when the pair $(c, p)$ occurs in $P$.
nodes.title: Parent relation of a list of pairs

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph and $R$ a list of root vertices, and run depth-first search on $G$ from $R$. Say that $p$ is a recorded parent of $c$ when the pair $(c, p)$ occurs in the list of (child, parent) pairs recorded by the search. Then there are no $k \ge 1$ and vertices $v_0, v_1, \dots, v_k$ with $v_k = v_0$ such that each $v_{i+1}$ is a recorded parent of $v_i$.
nodes.title: The DFS parent relation is acyclic

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph and $R$ a list of root vertices. The finish order (postorder) of the depth-first search of $G$ from $R$ contains no vertex twice.
nodes.title: DFS finishes each vertex at most once

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph given by ordered adjacency lists and let $R$ be a list of roots. If a vertex $v$ is reachable in $G$ from some root in $R$ by a directed path (possibly of length zero), then $v$ occurs in the preorder (discovery order) of the depth-first search of $G$ from $R$.
nodes.title: Depth-first search discovers every reachable vertex

nodes.summary: For every finite directed graph $G$ given by ordered adjacency lists and every list $R$ of roots, the preorder (discovery order) of the depth-first search of $G$ from $R$ contains no vertex twice.
nodes.title: Depth-first search discovers each vertex at most once

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph given by ordered adjacency lists and let $R$ be a list of roots. Every vertex in the preorder (discovery order) of the depth-first search of $G$ from $R$ is reachable in $G$ from some root in $R$ by a directed path (possibly of length zero).
nodes.title: Depth-first search discovers only reachable vertices

nodes.summary: Zero or more independent DFS machine steps.
nodes.title: Sequences of depth-first search machine steps

nodes.summary: A traversal over a vertex type $V$ consists of three lists: a preorder (discovery order) list of vertices, a postorder (finish order) list of vertices, and a list of parent pairs in $V \times V$, each stored as $(\text{child}, \text{parent})$.
nodes.title: Depth-first traversal record
Computer Science

can_prove.label: ready to prove
can_prove.meaning: Statement is in Lean and nothing it needs is blocked, so the proof can start.

can_state.label: ready to state
can_state.meaning: Everything its statement uses is in Lean, so the statement can be written in Lean.

conditional.label: conditionally proved
conditional.meaning: Proof compiles, but rests on an open statement without a recorded Lean proof.

fully_proved.label: fully proved
fully_proved.meaning: Proved, and every prerequisite is fully proved too.

inventory_checked.label: inventory checked
inventory_checked.meaning: Module inventory checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

inventory_pending.label: inventory pending
inventory_pending.meaning: Module inventory not yet checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

not_ready.label: not ready
not_ready.meaning: Needs more blueprint work before it can be attempted.

proved.label: proved
proved.meaning: Proof compiles, but something it rests on is not finished.

stated.label: statement formalized
stated.meaning: Statement is in Lean; the proof is not.
